item.title: Coreboot and the Lenovo T430
item.description: One of the things which I always wanted to do to my Lenovo T430 is to modify the BIOS to run CoreBoot. Coreboot is a freeware alternative that replaces a computer’s BIOS. One of the main advantages of running Coreboot is removing the whitelist for certain WLAN and WWAN cards. This has become a sticking point as WLAN cards move into 802.11ac and 802.11ax iterations. Yet another advantage, especially for privacy-minded individuals is the removal of the Intel Management Engine software that exists in many vendor ROMs and which has been shown to possess certain vulnerabilities.

I have been on the market for a new laptop ever since my old one gave up the ghost. My specifications are quite specific and in no order of importance :-

  • Not have a U series processor
  • 16GB of RAM

item.title: TP-Link TL-SG108E
item.description: I recently purchased a TP-Link TL-SG108E to augment my VLANed home network. I had trouble understanding the terminology of TP-Link’s VLAN configuration at first. According to its manual, there were 3 types of VLANs, namely, MTU, port-based and 802.1Q VLANs. MTU VLANs was interesting as it had nothing to do with the normal meaning of MTU (maximum transmission unit) in networks at all - it stood for Multi-Tenant Unit VLAN. According to the instruction manual, MTU VLAN (Multi-Tenant Unit VLAN) defines an uplink port which will build up several VLANswith each of the other ports. Each VLAN contains two ports, the uplink port and one of the other ports in the switch, so the uplink port can communicate with any other port but other ports cannot communicate with each other Port based was severely limited in its offering, as you could do only VLANS 2-8. Although it was enabled by default, VLANs were divided by port and that wasn’t really what I wanted. This meant that I had to use 802.1Q. To trunk (in Cisco’s terminology) a port, I needed to place all the ports in tagged mode to those VLANs. The equivalent in Cisco is to issue a switchport mode trunk command. To place a port in access mode, I had to put the port in untagged mode for the relevant VLAN and then put the VLAN ID into the 802.1Q PVID page of that port.

item.title: Link down on block
item.description: Today one of my fibre links to a particular school block went down. Nagios was screaming away bloody murder, emailing me constantly every 15 minutes. The link light on the connection was a steady orange I went up to the switch rack and checked both ends. The SFP convertor looked alright and there was no physical damage to the connecting fibre link, nor to the RJ45 cables connecting both access and distribution switches. The switches’ SNMP readout looked fine with no other errors whatsoever. The problem had to be software and not hardware. I rechecked the system logs and noticed that the port and the line conditions were down. This was confirmed by issuing the command “sh port GiX/X status”. I performed a “shutdown” and “no shutdown” on the port and the link went up immediately.

item.title: Virtual Private Servers
item.description: I had wanted to experiment with VPS solutions for quite a while now. VPS or virtual private servers is a hosted solution that have many advantages (and disadvantages) to normal web hosting solutions. They give you full root access to the server; this allows you to control the software installed on the machine and so the machine can be used for purposes other than web hosting. For example, some people use VPSes to run their Minecraft gaming server; others use them as a cheap(er) alternative to DropBox. The disadvantages of VPSes? You share the node with many other people as opposed to a dedicated server and you and you only can use. Many performance issues are a direct result of people abusing their usage of their VPS. Most hosts however do check for the existence of performance issues on their nodes and shutdown VMs that require too much CPU processing cycles or RAM. After much research, I went with a US VPS provider instead of a NZ one. Price was a major concern for me as this was for personal stuff and not work. Most local providers were charging between NZD $10 to $20 per month for an OpenVZ 512MB 20GB VM that was simply too small for my needs. I found a relatively good provider in the States that was charging only $30 per year - this price was more palatable to me. While the provider had a few bad online reviews, I decided to take the plunge. There were no more nodes available in Los Angeles so I had to settle for another location. Los Angeles is preferable for customers in the Asia/Pacific region due to lower latency. item.title: Moving away from Google's silo
item.description: After becoming an ardent fan of Google in the previous year, I had become more and more aware of its reach and control of data. Recent reports on its involvement in data gathering had become quite concerning to me and I was determined to wrest control of my data away from them. The last straw came when Google closed down Google Reader. This had become an important source of news for me and its closure meant that I had to look for alternatives. I decided to take this opportunity to take stock of what I had in the company and move the data away. Here were the alternatives I found. Google Drive - Dropbox Google Calendar - DaviCal and Mozilla Thunderbird Google Contacts - DaviCal and Mozilla Thunderbird Google Chrome - Mozilla Firefox Google Reader - TT-RSS reader (self-hosted) Google Maps - OpenStreetMaps Blogger - Wordpress The troublesome part was Google Reader; after searching for alternatives such as Feedly and The GoodReader, I wasn’t convinced that they were the right fit for my usage. I did a bit more digging and found TT-RSS which fit my needs perfectly. However, it requires self-hosting, installation and configuration which would be way beyond what a normal person would be capable of. This would stop me from recommending it as a alternative to Google Reader. I had been quite happy with my choices after running with them for a week or so. A lower reliance for Google services is always a good thing but this is tempered by the fact that I will need to maintain my own services.

item.title: My thoughts on the Chromebook Pixel
item.description: The Chromebook Pixel was recently announced by Google. Sporting an extremely high resolution touch screen and an Intel Core i5 processor, it resembles a high end laptop with its anodized aluminium finish and clean lines. And it has a high price to match - $1299 to be exact.Despite what some reviewers mentioned, I don’t think it looks like the MacBook Pro which is probably the target laptop that it is aimed at. It has a distinctive look to it, which can’t be said for the Samsung Chromebook. The latter looks just like an exact replica of the MacBook Air.I have trouble reconciling the price of this Chromebook with its intended usage pattern. At its heart, it runs ChromeOS, the exact same OS as the Samsung Chromebook which sells for $249. At that price, you would expect the Pixel to have some offline capability comparable to laptops running other operating systems at the same price point. But no, it has the same limitations as the other machines sporting ChromeOS.That then is the dilemma. Would it be worth the high end sticker price, even with the financial value of the 1TB of Google Drive storage thrown for free for 3 years into the mix? I don’t think so. Firstly, the state of web applications at this present time is still too immature for all types of applications to be ported natively. By all types, I would include the likes of multimedia editing software such as Adobe Photoshop and Adobe Premiere. We have not reached the level of sophistication required in these applications for web applications to completely replace their offline counterparts.Another problem hinted above is offline capability. At the time of writing, Quickoffice is offered together with the purchase of the Pixel, but with only limited editing capabilities. I’ve read it will take another 2 to 3 months for Google to refine the software to the point where it can seamlessly edit the offline document and sync with the online version on Google Drive. This is only a software update, and I expect this update to be offered to other Chromebooks in the forseeable future.I am left wondering what point Google is trying to make in announcing the Chromebook Pixel. Perhaps Google is trying to state that ChromeOS is not only for low end netbooks as is the case now, but it is also for the high end market. Or perhaps Google is testing the waters with its OEMs. Whatever the case, time will tell in revealing Google’s direction and strategy for ChromeOS.

item.title: The tablet
item.description:
I recently got a new tablet – the Samsung Galaxy Note 10.1. And I am loving it.

Recently, I thought of my usage habits on my phone and tablet. While the phone had been relegated back to voice calls, my main activity had always been on my Samsung Galaxy Tab 8.9. My surfing, checking of emails and usage of apps were primarily on the tablet even though both tablet and phone were Android and could run the same applications. Data was consumed on a level 3 to 4 times that of voice. And given the amount of voice calls I make per month, I will be lucky to even exceed $5 in a single month. With that in mind, it made a lot of sense to go with a tablet with phone functionality than a phablet. The emphasis here was screen size, and I had a lot of trouble previously with a touch interface on a 4.3″ screen. At the time of purchase, the Note series from Samsung had the 5.5″ (Note 2) and the 10.1″ (Note 10.1). There were confirmed rumours of the 8″ phablet (GT-N5100) as well. However, I decided to go with the 10.1 inch form factor as it offered the best value for money (both the Note 2 and the Note 10.1 were approximately the same price) and that the note-taking functions required more screen real estate than a 8″ or 5.5″. That is not to say that the Note 10.1 is without its disadvantages. The points I covered in my earlier post are still valid. That is, typing on a touch keyboard is a utter disgrace, the UI is inconsistent between applications and I would not be seen in public talking to a 10.1 inch tablet. The last point was a sticky one. It bothered me that I needed a solution to perform quality voice calls and also listen to music from the Note 10.1 without having to reach for an unsexy 10.1 inch tablet to control the music. Quality voice calls can only be gotten through noise-cancelling microphones and in the end, I opted for a Plantronics Voyager Legend which had not 2 but 4 noise-cancelling mics. It was quite cool to walk around with the Bluetooth headset and listen to voice prompts telling that the signal was weak or that the headset had lost connection. Listening to music was another issue altogether. I need something that could also do calls, since in theory, I could be in the middle of listening to music when a call arrives. The Sony Smart Headset Pro offered such a solution as it supported the Bluetooth A2DP profile. When I tested it, the Sony headset switched between the call and the music instantly without a hitch. The buttons on it could also control the active music player in the tablet so I could now leave the tablet in the bag. To top it off, it has an inbuilt MP3 player with a removable microSD card slot – good for those times when you want to save battery on the tablet. This together with the Samsung Chromebook is an unstoppable combination.

item.title: Garmin GPSes and corrupted maps
item.description: I use a Garmin Nuvi 2565 to help in travelling around and that GPS has saved my rear on more than one occasion. I brought it back with me on my travels to Singapore as my family and I were going to travel up to Johore Bahru for some R&R. It was working well until I loaded a corrupted gmapsupp.img into the system main memory. Upon a reboot, the system simply refused to load and was stuck at the ‘Loading maps’ screen. Cue Google to the rescue. An hour later yield many search results. Apparently, this was a very common complaint among Nuvi owners and the advice to many newbies was to simply put the new maps onto the removable microSD card. If ever the map was well and truly corrupted, one could simply remove the microSD card. But what if the map in question was in the unit’s main memory? A person wrote a Windows utility called Garmin Cure. What the utility does is to simply take a source firmware file for the GPS and convert it into a firmware that does nothing but present a UMASS storage device to the operating system once booted up. One could then delete away the offending file and then reflash it with the correct firmware. I tried it out. I first took an old firmware for the Nuvi 2565 (version 2.90) and converted it via Garmin Cure. I then launched the GPS into preboot mode by holding on to the top left hand corner of the LCD and pressing the power button at the same time. I then launched the firmware updater script which was able to then load the firmware to the unit. Windows 7 could then see the GPS as a drive and I was able to delete away the offending file. The unit was then subsequently flashed and updated with the correct firmware. A simple and well-written utility for the Garmin GPS. A must-have for any Garmin GPS owner.

item.title: SSL certificates

item.title: Google software replacements
item.description: I’ve been mulling around and deciding which software to use as replacements for my Google experience. The main objective around this project is to determine whether the current opensource tools are ready and have functionality equivalent to that of the Google applications. I am happy to say that for the most part, they are equivalent. A secondary aim is for privacy advocates – I am becoming increasingly disturbed over the prevalent use of tracking cookies, Google Adsense and social plugins in various websites, not least withstanding Google. And despite what has been put into the EULA, all these have the capability of tracking more than just one’s presence on the Internet. Let’s look at the list of software alternatives I concluded with in this exercise. Blogger – WordPress Google Reader – Tiny Tiny Reader GMail – Roundcube, PostFix, Dovecot Picasa – Gallery2 / Gallery3 Google Analytics – AWStats None of them were hard to set up, and with the exception of AWStats, all require only a database backend and a webserver frontend, The obvious stack to run all these was a LAMP one, with MySQL database and Apache webserver on a Centos machine. WordPress’ famous 5 minute installation truly lived up to its name, with Gallery2 coming not too far behind. The email portion was the hardest to implement, as it required manipulation of DNS records and prior knowledge of POP3/SMTP/IMAP and SPF/DKIM records. Would I recommend this for anyone? Yes, as with all things, if you are willing to dive deep into Unix / Linux and get your hands dirty, it’s a worthwhile experience. For the average person without a Unix background, no – it’s too troublesome and the steep learning curve will negate everything. It’s probably better in this case to go for a shared web hosting plan and using one of those quick installers on CPanel.

item.title: Samsung Chromebook
item.description: The Samsung Chromebook has been one of the more interesting purchases I’ve made this year. I started off with the Google ecosystem in mid 2004, using the Google search functionality and graduating to its email soon after. Before I knew it, I was becoming more and more entrenched in using its various services.Buying the Chromebook was a natural extension to this. Before I bought it, I did a bit of research. It seemed that Google intended its use to be a secondary computer, something that you would take around the home and use when the primary computer was off. To me, this made sense - there was no use duplicating the function of the primary machine.Now having the Chromebook in my hand and using it for 5 days, I will safely say that it serves the purpose of beng that secondary computer very well. Its form factor allowed me to use it in bed instead of being chained to the desk. As there was no internal cooling fan, I could use it until the wee hours of the morning without waking up my wife. The long battery life gave me the ability to use it without recharging for extended periods of time.Now you already get all those advantages with either a netbook or a tablet. What then is the difference amongst the three?Let’s start with the tablet. One of my biggest gripes with the tablet form factor is that it is an entertainment device first and foremost. Content creation is an afterthought, and until people find a way to make content creation easier on tablets, we will continue to have difficulty typing on glass. The Chromebook, on the other hand, has a laptop keyboard that looks suspiciously like that of the MacBook Air. That makes serious work on the Chromebook a complete joy.Another issue is the platform. Android as an operating system caters to both mobile phones and tablets, and there are definitely differences in UI design between the two. I am finding a lack of quality tablet applications as opposed to phone ones - its seems to me that most applications are designed for devices with small screen estate such as phones. While you can run phone apps on a tablet, the inefficiencies of doing so become apparent immediately once the app is opened. There is so much screen real estate in a tablet - and phone apps don’t take advantage of that.I had chanced upon a netbook before and while I found the form factor acceptable, its reliance on the x86 chip architecture meant that it was besottled with all the issues of that platform. This meant a hot running chipset, noise coming from the cooling fan and the excess baggage of a 20 year old hardware and software architecture. Intel has tried to rectify this to varying degrees of success with the Ultrabook initative but I don’t think they are going to go that far with it. A new methodology of using the Web requires a new approach from both hardware and software perspectives.Which is why I was so excited about the ARM Chromebook. It was the embodiment of the same form factor I was used to but coupled with a new (and old) usage philosophy. I say new and old too because actually the ARM processors have been around for quite a while but have matured to a point where it is today. The Chromebook’s minimalistic software is just enough to run the hardware and the browser and that’s it. That shows in the system’s boot times - I clocked it at 12 seconds from black screen to logon screen. It’s that fast.The Chromebook has supplanted my tablet as the main means of computing away from the desktop, but even more importantly, it has changed my entire thinking around local computing resources versus computing-as-a-service.We have definitely come a long way since the days of having to upgrade your system constantly. And I’m glad we have.

item.title: Solaris 11 Express upgrade
item.description: I had to upgrade one of our customer’s NAS units from Opensolaris 2009.06 to Solaris 11 Express during the Christmas holidays. Solaris 11 Express is build 151, and Opensolaris 2009.06 is build 111.It was actually a painless task; it’s well documentated in the release notes, and is one of the supported upgrade paths from Opensolaris 2009.06. I needed to upgrade to build 134b as an intermediate step along the way though.However, like all IT upgrades, there were a few chinks …a. No preservation of network linksThe upgrade process did not preserve the bonded network interfaces. I had to redo the entire dladm thingie. Quite trivial, but the upgrade from Opensolaris 2009.06 to v134b preserved that, so why didn’t the upgrade from v134b to Solaris 11 Express?b. iSCSIApparently, the normal ISCSI command “zfs set shareiscsi=on zpool01” is no longer available in Solaris 11 Express. In fact, the property is no longer there …. You will have to enable COMSTAR and use the commands itadm, sdbadm and stmfadm to configure the LUN target and add the zvol to that target. It’s quite trivial, but I would have thought that everything (like SMB and NFS) was integrated with ZFS.c. /etc/default/nfsNo more of that /etc/default/nfs file. Everything is now managed through sharectl. So in order to see the properties of NFS, you will have to issue the command “sharectl get nfs”.I was impressed with Solaris 11 Express, notwithstanding these issues, but I am beginning to wonder what Solaris will be like under Oracle’s tenure.

item.title: Finding use for old thin clients
item.description: I recently found an old Wyse S10 terminal that was built circa 2001. 4 USB ports, 1 VGA port, a 10/100mbps network port as well as a serial port. Not too bad connectivity options for a box that’s like 10 times smaller than my computer. Completely no moving parts - the system boots from a flash ROM on the motherboard.Being the Mr Geek that I was, I immediately started to take it apart.The first thing that struck me was that although there was a 44pin IDE connector on the motherboard, there was absolutely no space for a 1.8" SSD or HDD inside the casing. Whatever this thing boots from will have to be external.I did a bit of research and found out that the system can boot from USB; this setting was present in the BIOS. Getting into the BIOS was another problem, as you have to press the Del key at just the right instant. Eventually I did and so I modified the setting to boot from USB first, PXE second and lastly, the IDE connection.Then came the question of what OS to boot. Actually, which linux distribution was the more pertinent question. In the end, Tiny Core Linux came to mind, and soon enough, TCL was there running on the Wyse terminal in all its glory.I was actually quite impressed with the speed of it, considering the fact that it’s running a AMD Geode processor at 366Mhz. item.title: Linux and SRSS 4.2
item.description: Yesterday, I managed to debug why the USB thumbdrives don’t work across a failover group for the Linux version of SRSS 4.2. This problem had been irking me since we deployed SRSS 4.2 at a customer site, and the users suddenly found themselves without USB thumbdrive and serial access.On a pure SRSS 4.2 SLES10SP2 machine, I issued the following command :-server# netstat -n | grep 7011tcp 0 1 10.1.1.61:40860 67.2.1.10:7011 SYN_SENTtcp 0 1 10.1.1.61:40890 67.2.1.10:7011 SYN_SENTtcp 0 1 10.1.1.61:40787 66.2.1.10:7011 SYN_SENTPort 7011 is used by utdevmgrd in connecting with the remote Sunrays in establishing device connections, specifically USB, parallel and serial. Something was sent, but no reply was received by the server.Obviously, something weird was going on; the destination IP addresses were inverted; that explained why DTUs couldn’t connect to utdevmgrd via port 7011. utdevmgrd was thus unable to create the symlinks for $UTDEVROOT to be functional EXCEPT for the server that the DTU originally connected to.I replaced /opt/SUNWut/lib/utdevmgrd with the version available in SRSS 4.1 patch 139550-04, and viola, it works out of the box. :Dtcp 0 0 10.1.2.61:40301 10.1.2.65:7011 ESTABLISHEDtcp 0 0 10.1.2.61:40006 10.1.2.67:7011 ESTABLISHEDtcp 0 0 10.1.2.61:40183 10.1.2.69:7011 ESTABLISHEDIt’s just one of those weird things which happens in the course of my work.

item.title: Sunray 5 kiosk scripts
item.description: I found that in SRSS 4.2, $UTDEVROOT was not referenced properly. The location field can then be extracted from the ‘utdesktop’ output as is usually the case.# Sunray 4.1theMACAddr=cd $UTDEVROOT; /bin/pwd | sed 's/.*\(............\)/\1/'theLocation=/opt/SUNWut/sbin/utdesktop -o | grep $theMACAddr | awk -F,'{print $2;}'# Sunray 4.2MYDISP=echo $DISPLAY | awk -F: '{print $2}' | awk -F. '{print $1}'theMACAddr=grep TERMINAL /tmp/SUNWut/config/dispinfo/$MYDISP | awk -F. '{print $2}'theLocation=/opt/SUNWut/sbin/utdesktop -o | grep $theMACAddr | awk -F, '{print $2;}'

item.title: Social networks, viruses and spam
item.description: Recently, the spam problem hit very near home when my uncle’s laptop got infected with a trojan. A Norton Antivirus product caught and flagged the intrusion. The offending exe was downloaded from a link contained within a Facebook message that was sent out from my (hacked) brother-in-law’s account.Upon closer inspection, it was clear what had happened. The executable masqueraded as an upgrade to the Norton Antivirus product, thus leading to the activation of the trojan and its subsequent takeover of the computer.I immediately terminated the process and removed the directory. In addition to that, I checked the registry settings to ensure that the executable didn’t leave anything untowards that might contribute to another infection. One was bad enough.That event started me thinking on the role of social conditioning in the realm of computer viruses. Traditionally, viruses have been reliant on trusts between computers. That is, a trust relationship between 2 computers is taken advantage of by a virus in infecting its hosts.However, with the advent of social networking, viruses are taking advantage of the trust not between 2 computers, but the recipient AND the sender of a message. In this case, a Facebook message that was deemed trustworthy to be read contained a deadly payload that infected the recipient’s machine.Admittedly, this approach is not new. Trojans and viruses with the ability to parse through address lists and send messages through have been around for eons. But social networks present a whole new opportunity for virus and trojan writers.Don’t let them catch you.

item.title: Google Chromium OS
item.description: One of my pet projects now is researching into lightweight desktop environments. It’s not really an operating system per se, as most, if not all of these environments run on top of Linux. Desktop enviroments are just that - environments that provide the user an area to work on.Google Chromium was the first one under the microscope. Having followed the instructions from Google, I compiled the OS under Ubuntu 9.10 and subsequently dumped the image onto a 2GB thumbdrive. Booting the laptop with it was a simple matter of adjusting the BIOS to boot from USB and sticking the thumbdrive in. Switched on the laptop and off it went.To be honest, there’s a lot to like about Chromium. A simplistic user interface, fast Javascript execution and Flash compatibility means that any user can pick up a netbook and use the Web in a matter of seconds (12 seconds, actually). I can envision a whole gathering of old people using their netbooks without having to ask for guidance. That’s cool.But I’m not sure for other users. Take, for example, power users. Power users like me would want to use more than just the Web even if that netbook is a secondary PC. We would want to tinker with the innards, use 3G broadband or even watch a DIVX movie or two on the netbook. All these you can’t do at this stage of development.So I wiped off the Google Chromium OS build on my laptop. It just didn’t fit the bill for me.

item.title: Cloud computing
item.description: In the office, we have had quite a few heated discussions on the advent of cloud computing, and how it will change the computing landscape over the next decade. And it’s already happening as we speak.It all started when Google launched their Chromium OS, and one of us decided to compile the source code and stick it into a USB thumbdrive. We watched the OS boot up in approximately 12 seconds, and was presented with a beautiful simplistic interface - the web browser.One of my colleagues then asked what the point of this was, when you could very well run a thick OS instead of a thin one, and have the advantages of being able to run thick applications at the same time. With a thin OS, you could only run applications off the web interface, nothing more, nothing less.I believe this argument will not die off, but will continue to stay with us as long as computers are a part of our lives. Just like how men always argue that the women say that their husbands never listen to them. :)Although the push for cloud computing presents certain risks such as security and accessibility, it represents a conceptual leap in that applications and services are now not necessarily part of your organisational domain, and that these very apps and services could be offered by some entity outside of the domain.And it’s not just Google moving into this. Take, for example, an educational instituion. A school may say, “hey, let’s host some applications and deliver them through the web for the students to use at home.” In this case, the school becomes the application provider, and thus, an agent in the whol arena of cloud computing. And I already know of some schools delivering these services.Whether that approach is an appropriate one remains to be seen.

item.title: The (Holy) OS Wars
item.description: My colleague and I have been talking about the holy wars in IT - wars that involves people’s preferences of operating systems. Unfortunately, these wars are happening frequently everyday; for proof, just look at the IT forums on the Internet. For some people, it turns into a religious war full of name-calling with insults and mud-pie thrown at each other’s faces.One of my friends happens to be like that. He is totally convinced that the OS he’s using is the best in the entire world, and nothing else comes even close to the reliability, stability and robustness of the platform. When given alternatives, he would shrug them off, saying that “that OS is a piece of crap”.Luckily, we are both on very good terms, so although we do get into a discussion on the pros and cons of each OS, we don’t get that far that we launch into … errrm … a full scale heated discussion. :D But for me, I have a somewhat different approach to the whole subject at hand.I prefer to think of the whole environment as an ecosystem, and each operating system occupying its niche inside it. Windows is an extremely mature desktop operating system, and it operates as such where others don’t foot the bill. Linux and Solaris are excellent for server grade stuff, things that you want to run 24/7 without interruptions and crashes. OS X is brillant for DTP and graphic design houses. And the list goes on.One interesting thing about being a Unix engineer is that I get to touch many different distributions of *nixes. A particular aspect that I have come to appreciate is the power of open source and its effect on software. A prime example is the desktop environment : right now, I’m using OpenSolaris on my laptop with Gnome as its desktop environment, and it is remarkably … no, make that exactingly, similar to the Ubuntu machine I have at my work desktop that also has Gnome. To me, that shows the flexibility of open source and how it has allowed software to be ported and integrated into different operating systems.And yet, I am vividly aware of the fact that despite those similarities, OpenSolaris and Ubuntu remain very different beasts under the hood, each with its own strengths and weaknesses. Just take a look at the Unix Rosetta Stone to see the differences. And so the same goes for not just OpenSolaris and Ubuntu, but also Mac OSX, Windows XP and Windows 7.Thus, it is pointless to argue whether any OS is better than the other if the needs are not explained in the first place. To me, the strengths of that OS can and will qualify it for the environment’s needs. All in all, the OS with the most strengths is the one that is most appropriate for that workload.

item.title: OpenSolaris on the HP 6710b

item.title: Email server crash
item.description: This week has proven to be a really busy week. First it was a server crash at site A, then just today I had another server crash at site B. It’s really just my luck to have so many server crashes this week.Today’s episode involved an email server running Zimbra that lived within a VM in ESXi 3.5. The server crashed due to the lack of space in the root directory. Essentially that meant 100% in /, which is suicidal in the Linux world. How that eluded me is a question waiting to be answered, as I thought I did check the space and that percentage hung around 83% yesterday. (How that went to 100% in 8 hours is anybody’s guess.)So I had to restore the entire system from backup. That was trivial thanks to zfs, a filesystem developed by Sun, and its snapshotting features. As I set it to snapshot the filesystem every 12 hours, I was able to recover all the files dating from yesterday night.Once I checked the logs, I knew what went wrong in the install. I assumed that Zimbra stored its email queues like everybody else in /var/run or /var/spool. Instead, Zimbra stores its email queue directly under /opt. Now that wouldn’t matter to anyone who specifies a huge directory like 100GB for /opt. But it doesn’t work for people like who like to partition directories according to their usage. Obviously, I was in a lot of trouble.I quickly created a new 150GB filesystem on /dev/sdb1, did a mkfs.ext3 on it, and Zimbra went straight into it. Started Zimbra via zmcontrol start, and off it went.It was like a dream come true to see the UI once again.

item.title: Solaris LDOMs and containers
item.description: Recently, I’ve been playing around with Solaris LDOMs on a T2000 loan unit. LDOMs are very much a software extension of the physical hardware domains found in the mid and high range Sun servers. It’s quite cool to be able to assign a domain to particular resources on the system, and then start, stop and reboot that domain independent on other domains.One application that I could forsee happening is the application of containers within LDOMs. Containers (or zones), another Solaris peculiarity, are like FreeBSD jails - they allow you to partition in the OS a section that is unaffected by the rest of the OS - a so-called boundary. While this by itself is rather unexciting, the concept of branded zones is quite the reverse.Branded zones allow the emulation of an OS environment. Here comes the real kicker. It is possible to migrate a Solaris 8 machine (with little or no change) and put that into a Solaris 8 container within an LDOM. That means that mulitple old legacy machines running Solaris 8 could be migrated whole-sale into containers in a Solaris 10 machine with no change to application code.Cost and time savings? You betcha …

item.title: Auto negotiation? Nah ...
item.description: Recently, I have become a little perturbed by the network performance of one of my customer sites. I kept receiving complaints of poor external network connectivity, one which didn’t make sense when you take into consideration a line speed of 2mbps ADSL. Even when the internet company graciously decided to raise the speed to 5mbps, there were complaints of network dropouts.So last Friday, I and my colleague decided to do some network testing. We did some MTU fragmentation tests to determine the maximum packet size. The result (1272) fell within the norm of most networks, and there wasn’t really anything wrong. However, we immediately discovered that the packet loss from the internal network to the next outside hop was unbearably high - the percentage of loss was almost 40% in some instances. This was extremely bad, and we knew we had to find the source of the problem.We did a lot of tests on the firewall, which was the device nearest to the outside cloud. To make things more confusing, all tests from the outside world to the firewall resulted in packet loss, while that from the outside world to the edge device (before our firewall) resulted in no packet loss. This was getting weirder by the minute.To cut a long story short, my colleague and I later discovered that the edge routing device that the internet provider had installed was operating at 10mbps full duplex, not the 100mbps full duplex rating that they provided us to put into our firewall. The mismatch in the operating speeds meant that our firewall downgraded itself to the lowest possible speed grade (10mbps half duplex) in order to safeguard itself. Well, it did, and in so doing causing tremendous packet loss.Packet loss affects network performance because if the receiving end terminates the session abruptly, the sending end will have to send the entire frame again. When this happens over, say, 1000 users, you get network congestion and invariably slow application response. Definitely not good, to say the least.

item.title: Troubles with SQL Server
item.description: I had a lot of fun today with SQL Server 2005. One of my colleagues received an urgent phonecall from an IT manager from this company. The guy on the other end had a frantic tone to his voice, and I soon learned why - his database Server had crashed, and users were unable to access the Point-of-Sales application which depended on the database server. Naturally, the first thing he did was to call us - his IT point of contact.Unfortunately for my colleague, he didn’t have any experience with SQL Server at all, and so he referred the problem to me. He literally pulled me (and my chair) and wheeled me to his table - I gave him a dirty look as he was doing that. :) I was in the middle of decoding some permissions issue at my client’s place, and which took a bit of concentration to do, so of course I was a little annoyed …. grin.He proceeded to explain the problem to me. I asked him one question.Me : How did the server crash?Colleague : The server was doing a reboot which was forced by Windows Update. It crashed while loading the device drivers.Me : sighLuckily for me, I do have experience with MS SQL Server from projects with my previous company. Most of them were using MS SQL Server 2000, and 2005 shouldn’t that much of a difference.I then proceeded to check the mdf and ldf files holding the application data. All good. That meant that I could unregister the existing database and reattach the files back without loosing any data in the process. One thing which I had stressed to him (and even in my previous company) was that we as the systems integrator are responsible for data integrity and not the data itself. There is definitely a difference between the 2, and we cannot be held liable for the latter.I used EMS SQL Manager liteware to restore the databases after checking for free space on the HDD. It was very quick - 5 minutes later, our client was up and running. I checked the transactional logs, and funnily enough, nothing seemed amiss. He didn’t even call us back for the rest of the day.And I got scolded by my colleague for performing the fix so fast that he couldn’t watch and learn what I was doing. Heh heh … sigh

item.title: Sun Storage 7110 update
item.description: Ahh … I finally managed to find the solution to that storage issue I was facing at Te Puke.The Sun Storage 7110 was running the Solaris CIFS service which enabled Windows machines to see the SMB shares. The problem was that although the system could join the domain, it could not authenticate to the DC, with the end-result that it could only see security principals on itself and not the domain.After 4 hours of gingerly poking around, I figured out that nothing was wrong with the AD controller, and focused all my attention on the storage box. It was then that I discovered that the storage box was deliberately parsing only the first 16 characters of the domain. I downloaded a system update for the Solaris box and after installation, voila, the domain security principals could be seen.I must have been the happiest man alive when I saw that … haa haa … Probably a reminder to self : remember to apply all software updates before implementation. :)

item.title: LDAP Server failure
item.description: One of my customer sites experienced a catastrophic server failure, with the primary LDAP authentication server going down first and the rest daisy-chaining after that.A quick look at the message logs didn’t reveal anything unusual, and restores from backups didn’t help at all. I began to suspect something wrong with the program’s databases, and deleted them away, and recreated them after backing up the customer’s LDAP datastores on the secondary LDAP server.Voila. But that was after a whole day of deciphering where it went wrong.A few lessons which I’ve learnt along the way.1. It’s never good to try to restore from backup immediately, but it does pay to understand the problem and to rectify it.2. A secondary LDAP server is a must for any site. That was the saving grace and provided me the means to restore the site quickly.3. It’s not good to do a backup of the LDAP server through an export of the LDIF file. It’s a lot better to backup the entire directory server instance.Hope it won’t happen again.

item.title: Sunrays as compared to other thin clients
item.description: Yesterday, I attended a seminar organised by one of our vendors together with a colleague. Most of the people were from the storage and virtualisation industry, as the seminar was geared mainly for the big thing in IT, virtualisation. The big players, IBM, Lenovo, VMWare, EMC and Symantec were there, and so were the smaller ones such as Datastor, Storagecraft and Novell. Each had their own particular product to market, and as expected in such a seminar, product hard-selling is quite common amongst all the booths I visited.One of these booths is this company called Wyse. Wyse markets thin clients, which puts it in a position directly competing with mine which sells thin clients as well. I was a little kay poh and decided to walk over to their booth for a little look see. The technology is quite impressive and delivers a lot of features to the consumer. And even the presenter was (in my opinion) doing a bit of Sunray bashing once he knew which company I was from.Which brings me to the point of this post. What really distinguishes the Sunray from the other thin clients such as the Wyse-s and HPs?Firstly, power consumption. All thin clients consume much less power than a normal PC, but Sunrays only consume 4 watts of power compared to around 6.6 watts for a Wyse S10 or 14.1 watts for a V10L. Doesn’t seem like much, but quickly add up all those watts in a mission-critical environment, and those watts won’t seem so small after all.Secondly, complexity. Sun only offers 3 models of thin clients (Sunray 2FS, Sunray 2, and Sunray 270), while Wyse offers many more models, 14 if I remember correctly. If there has to be some many models in the product range, there surely needs to be some level of maintenance within the machines themselves. The Sunrays on the other hand are only client display devices and thus require absolutely zero maintenance. We have a few first generation Sunrays sitting in our office and they still work as well as the second generation devices.Thirdly, in the strictest sense of the word, Wyse thin clients are not really thin clients but embedded devices. You will definitely need to patch the clients’ embedded OSes. In contrast, the Sunrays only contain enough logic to do display graphics and network, but that’s about it. No embedded WinXPe or WinCE to manage. There’s some implications to security here, but it’s probably arguable. After all, what can you do with a hacked thin terminal???I’m not bashing the Wyse thin clients, and in fact, the Sunrays have issues (isochronous USB devices such as webcams come to mind) of their own which the Wyses do not face. The Wyse thin clients, together with the TCX accompanying software, deliver quite a bit of desktop functionality, with multimedia and USB redirection.An aside at this juncture. I do see some culture shock on the part of some people when they first encounter the Sunray and its limitations but I think all that can be easily overcome through user education and other methods. Frankly, what worries me most about the Sunrays is the fact that Oracle has now bought Sun, and what its committment to Sun’s various projects, which includes the Sunray, still remains an unknown.But I’m sure (and hopeful) that the market is big enough for 4 or more thin client manufacturers … :)

item.title: Solaris 8 and the Netra 240
item.description: As can been seen from the recent twitters, Mr Geek has been tinkering around with a Netra 240 Sparc box lately. One of our customers has decided to do some stuff around an old version of SAP, and so Mr Geek, being a Solaris/Linux engineer on the team, was tasked to see how best to do it.Actually, it was quite a heady task. When the server first came, there was no CDROM drive located on it. That meant a Solaris Jumpstart installation; I used an existing Sun Ultra 10 workstation as a boot/install server and configured the necessary services to run it (in.rarpd, rpc.bootparams, nfs, in.tftpd, rpcbind, mountd).The first time we tried the jumpstart, the Netra simply refused to boot, giving a kernel error. At first, I couldn’t figure out what was happening, and I even trawled through the log files, looking for clues to ascertain the cause of it. It took a long time, but eventually, I traced it to a hardware-related function. The Netra 240 had a Sparc 1.5Ghz chip, and the only version of Solaris 8 certified to run on it was Solaris 8 07/03. And I was using Solaris 8 07/01. Sigh.We were lucky enough to have our company contacts provide for us the appropriate version of Solaris 8, and we proceeded to test it out. Yep, the jumpstart worked perfectly, and I loaded the entire distribution (SUNWCall) onto the disk after partitioning it.Next came the tape autoloader. I was provided a Sun SL48 tape autoloader and it had a fibre-channel (FC) connection on it. I connected it to the Qlogic FC card already installed on the Netra, did a devfsadm -v -c to configure it to recognise the tape drive, touch /reconfigure and a final init 6 to reboot the server.Nada. No /dev/rmt entries.Sigh. Back to good old Google.So I researched out the topic, and it seems that Solaris 8 does not have the inbuilt capabilities required for FC SAN/tape drive connectivity while Solaris 10 does. I sniffed out the packages required for it to work, and they include a whole load of device drivers and Solaris 8 system patches in a piece of software called Sun Storedge. Ah good. I downloaded the whole lot, and proceeded to install it.One final reboot, and I could see all the /dev/rmt entries sitting nicely waiting to be used.I’m one happy camper. :)

item.title: Tape autoloader commandline control

item.title: LDAP issue resolved ... finally!!!!
item.description: Yes, I (finally) solved the LDAP issue that has been troubling me for the past few weeks.The issue was that I couldn’t get the native Solaris LDAP client to recognise the Sun Enterprise Directory Server that I was using. And all this despite my being able to join the Solaris LDAP client to the domain controller.After a lot of troubleshooting and reading of error logs over 3 days, I managed to nail the problem.It turns out that the Solaris LDAP client is set up to recognise user and groups with the attributes posixAccount and posixGroup respectively.And even the group within which the user accounts reside must be called ou=People.Once I added these objectclasses to each individual account, the LDAP client worked perfectly. I also created 2 organisational units for each suborganisation to further sub-divide the users and groups.

item.title: LDAP issues
item.description: In the current project I’m leading right now, I was faced with an interesting issue - integrating a Solaris LDAP client with a Sun Enterprise Directory server running on SUSE Linux 10 SP1.Now, Solaris’ LDAP client behaves very differently from Linux’s OpenLDAP client, so much so as to warrant a whole treatment on the subject. But that’s for another day.Anyway, I took a look at the log files.findBaseDN: ldap not runningfindBaseDN: calling __ns_ldap_default_config()found 1 namingcontextsfindBaseDN: __ns_ldap_list(NULL,"(&(objectclass=nisDomainObject)(nisdomain=xxx.xxxx.nz))“rootDN[0] dc=xxxx,dc=xxxxx,dc=nzNOTFOUND:Could not find the nisDomainObject for DN dc=xxxx,dc=xxxx,dc=nzfound_cxt = -1findBaseDN: Err exitFailed to find defaultSearchBase for domain xxxx.xxxx.nzsnippet>Darn, the stupid LDAP client expects to find an NIS domain first BEFORE parsing it to reveal the LDAP domain. sighI then inserted the attributes that were required (nisDomainObject key and nisDomain attribute) into the baseDN.And presto,bash-3.00# ldapclient manual \ > -a domainName=xxxxx.xxxx.nz \ > -a defaultSearchBase=dc=xxxx,dc=xxxx,dc=nz \ > 10.x.x.xxSystem successfully configured#>What a lovely result.

item.title: VMware performance hit
item.description: One question posed to me is whether there is a performance impact from putting so many of such VMs on top of an OS. This question really touches on how the VM hypervisor functions.Many people are acquainted with VMs only through their association with VM Player and/or VM Workstation, which involves the VM software running on top of a host OS. In this case, there is definitely a performance hit as all the guest OSes contend for the same resources as the host OS.However, VMware ESX involves running the guest OSes on ‘bare metal’; as the name implies, the OS itself is optimised to such an extent that only the bare minimum is installed. In most cases, the performance hit is roughly to the order to 5% to 10%, if not more.Anandtech has a good article on the various technologies adopted by different companies. Of these, IMHO, Xen and VMware are the ones to watch.

item.title: VMWare Applicances on servers
item.description: I’m been arrowed to do a DR project based on an implementation of VMWare ESX server. One of the many interesting questions I have been posed is this : what is the optimum number of VM appliances that one can place in a single box?There is no hard and fast rule to the number of VM appliances, and as such, different people will give different answers to this question. I suppose in my case, my answer is this :-For heavy load VMs, 15 to 20 of such VMs can co-exist in a box.For small to medium load VMs, 30 to 50 of such VMs can coexist.There is no established way currently to measure the thresholds of such VMs; indeed, I believe VMware is only beginning to establish a benchmark called VMmark to benchmark VM performance. All I can say is that such numbers are only gotten through trial and error as well as gut feelings. It is hard to qualify and quantify such experiences.Put too few VMs in a box, and one purpose of implementing VMs is defeated, which is to maximise the usage of resources (which will be otherwise wasted) within that box. Put too many, and you are faced with the perennial problem of putting too many eggs in one basket. A single hardware failure will cause a ripple effect through all the appliances in that system.Virtualisation is set to be the next big thing in server computing. But only time will tell on what norms the industry will adopt, such as the number of appliances per server. And until then, I guess everyone will be fighting over this in the various projects implementing VMs.

item.title: Undeleting files in Ubuntu Linux
item.description: Foremost is a console program to recover files based on their headers, footers, and internal data structures. This process is commonly referred to as data carving. Foremost can work on image files, such as those generated by dd, Safeback, Encase, etc, or directly on a drive. The headers and footers can be specified by a configuration file or you can use command line switches to specify built-in file types. These built-in types look at the data structures of a given file format allowing for a more reliable and faster recovery.Originally developed by the United States Air Force Office of Special Investigations and The Center for Information Systems Security Studies and Research , foremost has been opened to the general publicsource code at http://foremost.sourceforge.net/Grab foremost:sudo apt-get install foremostHave Foremost audit your drive for recoverable files:sudo foremost -w -i /dev/hda -o /recovery/foremostHave foremost recover jpg files:sudo foremost -t jpg -i /dev/hda -o /recovery/foremost

item.title: Windows on Linux?
item.description: Many people have seen me use Windows applications on my Ubuntu 7.10 laptop, and were even amazed of it happening. There is definitely a technology out there that allows you to do so, and it comes in the form of WINE.No, not the sort of stuff that gets you high, drowsy and want to dance on the bartop with a bikini clad girl. WINE stands for ‘WINE is not an emulator’. WINE is a cross-compatibility library software that allows Windows applications to run on Linux, often without modification. And it works by translating Windows API calls from software to Linux API calls and vice versa. There is only a slight performance hit, but one that is barely noticable.WINE comes in useful for me as most of my office’s documents, understandably come in the form of MS Office documents. OpenOffice 2.3 still has issues with complex documents, and its Spreadsheet app cannot accept Excel VBA macros. Thus, I use WINE to run MS Office and read these documents.WINE is not just limited to 2D applications. I have seen people run 3D accelerated games such as World of Warcraft on their Linux boxes.So the next time you run Linux on your box, do have this thought in mind that you are not just limited to those Linux applications; you are also able to run Windows applications as well.How’s that for cross-compatibility?

item.title: Linux commands - network

item.title: Difference between SAN, NAS and DAS
item.description: This is a really good picture illustrating the differences between the 3 storage types. One can easily get confused over the terminology, and even the technology.DAS = Direct Attached Storage. These are disks that are physically located in your host machine. NAS = Network Attached Storage. NAS is file based. For example a CIFS or NFS share. This is typically TCP/IP based access. The NAS device owns the data on it. That is, the NAS device administers the data. For example, you connect to a NAS device from a windows machine by accessing \servername\share. SAN = Storage Area Network. SAN is block based. This is when LUNs (logical unit numbers) are involved on a host. The host owns the data. The host is in charge of the partition, formating, and access to the LUN. You can access a SAN via two protocols: iSCSI (TCP/IP) and/or Fiber Channel (FC).Hope this helps.

item.title: Switch ACLs versus Firewalls
item.description:
I have been thinking about this topic ever since a particular issue erupted over at one of my customers’ premises during a meeting. The issue at hand was the deployment of a Layer 3 switch at a network topology where a firewall should be deployed. Should a switch with ACLs be used, or perhaps a firewall be in a better position to handle the job?

Ever since vendors started deploying multiple feature sets in their product lines, the lines drawn between switches, routers and firewalls have steadily become blurrier and blurrier. Firewalls can now do dynamic routing, and switches can even achieve packet inspection at wirespeed. Where can the line be drawn at deploying either a switch or a firewall?

item.title: Google Browser Sync
item.description: For those of you who switch between different computers all the time, you may have found it frustrating to transfer your browser settings. Fear not, Google has a utility to help you do exactly that. This plugin works only for Firefox. It uses your account at Google to help store your cookies, bookmarks, history and if you choose, even your saved passwords. You can choose to encrypt the data being transferred to Google as well. Google Browser Sync is completely automated. The settings you select at startup are automatically synchronized across each of the computers on which you install Browser Sync. You won’t even need to log in every time you start the browser. You can change which browser components are being synced – or even stop the syncing process entirely – using the settings panel in the upper-right corner of the page. The settings panel also gives you access to your PIN.
